summary: This informational RFC describes Virtual Subnet, a solution built on BGP/MPLS IP VPNs that extends a subnet across locations. It can be used to build Layer 3 network virtualization overlays within or between data centers.

eli5.summary: It makes machines in different buildings look like they are on the same street, even though they are far apart.

questions: bgp mpls ip vpn data center
how to extend subnet across locations
subtitle: Extend a subnet across data centers using BGP/MPLS IP VPNs

tldr.problem: Virtual machines migrating between data centers need to keep their IP addresses, which means extending a subnet across geographically distant locations. Layer 2 approaches do not scale with millions of VMs, and cause flooding and ARP cache issues.
tldr.mechanism: Virtual Subnet reuses BGP/MPLS IP VPN technology to advertise host routes between data centers, with ARP proxy services on the PE routers to respond to ARP requests. Hosts in different data centers appear to be on the same subnet, but traffic between them uses Layer 3 routing inside the VPN.
tldr.outcome: Layer 3 subnet extension scales better than Layer 2, reduces flooding, and avoids ARP cache table bloat, but cannot support non-IP traffic or IP broadcast.

today: RFC 7814 remains a current informational resource for data center operators and service providers considering Layer 3 subnet extension. It has not been obsoleted and describes an actively used approach for multi-data-center connectivity.

sections.title: The Data Center Problem
sections.content:
Cloud providers host thousands of virtual machines (VMs) across multiple data centers and need to migrate VMs without changing their IP addresses. To allow this without renumbering servers, the subnet containing those VMs must extend across data centers.

Traditional Layer 2 network extension (Ethernet bridging) faces serious scalability challenges when millions of VMs are involved. Data-center switches would need to learn both local and remote MAC addresses, bloating forwarding tables. Gateway routers would accumulate enormous ARP cache tables as the number of remote hosts grows. Flooding of ARP and unknown unicast traffic across data centers would degrade performance. Virtual Subnet addresses these problems by using Layer 3 routing inside a VPN instead of Layer 2 bridging.
sections.eli5: When your computers move between buildings, they need the same address. But connecting buildings with a bridge does not work when there are millions of computers, because every device needs to remember every address everywhere.

sections.title: How Virtual Subnet Works
sections.content:
Virtual Subnet leverages BGP/MPLS IP VPNs (RFC 4364), a mature technology operators already use. Provider Edge (PE) routers at each data center run a Virtual Routing and Forwarding (VRF) instance for the extended subnet. When a host connects locally, the PE router creates a host route for that host (e.g., 192.0.2.3/32) and advertises it via BGP to remote PE routers.

Each PE router enables ARP proxy on the interfaces connected to its local hosts. When a host sends an ARP request for another host on the virtual subnet, the local PE responds with its own MAC address. The host then sends packets destined for the remote host to its local PE. The PE tunnels the packets through the MPLS backbone to the remote PE, which forwards them to the actual destination host. From the hosts' perspective, they are on the same subnet, but traffic travels as Layer 3 routed packets inside the VPN.
sections.eli5: Each building has a secretary (PE router) who knows about computers in other buildings. When a computer asks for another building's computer, the secretary says 'send it to me' and tunnels it there.

sections.title: Benefits and Capabilities
sections.content:
Scalability: Data-center switches learn only local MAC addresses, not remote ones, so forwarding tables stay bounded. PE routers hold only ARP entries for their own local hosts, so ARP cache tables do not grow with the number of data centers.

Reduced flooding: Flooding of unknown unicast, ARP, and multicast is confined to each data center. This dramatically reduces inter-data-center bandwidth waste and improves performance.

Multicast support: Multicast VPN (MVPN) technologies can be applied without modification to support IP multicast between hosts on the virtual subnet.

Host mobility: When a VM migrates, the PE router to which it now connects creates a new host route and advertises it. The old PE withdraws its route. Gratuitous ARP or unsolicited Neighbor Discovery messages notify other hosts of the change.

Reuses proven technology: Service providers already run BGP/MPLS VPNs for customer services and can apply the same operational knowledge to Virtual Subnet.
sections.eli5: Each building only remembers its own computers. Messages to far buildings go through a tunnel. VMs can move between buildings and everything still works. No magic, just good organization.

sections.title: What It Cannot Do
sections.content:
No non-IP traffic: Virtual Subnet is strictly Layer 3. Legacy clustering applications that rely on non-IP protocols (e.g., heartbeat over proprietary links) are not supported. Operators can use a hybrid Layer 2/Layer 3 approach to bridge non-IP traffic while routing IP traffic.

No broadcast or link-local multicast: Intra-subnet traffic travels as routed packets, so IP broadcast messages and link-local multicast (e.g., mDNS) cannot cross data centers. Again, a hybrid approach can forward these at Layer 2.

Traceroute visibility: Because intra-subnet traffic is routed at Layer 3, traceroute output reveals PE routers between hosts on the same subnet, breaking the illusion that they are directly connected. Applications that set TTL to 1 for same-subnet communication may fail unless special TTL handling is deployed.
sections.eli5: It only works for regular internet traffic, not special protocols. Broadcasts do not cross buildings. Tracing the path shows you the tunnels, not a direct connection.

sections.title: Security and Deployment
sections.content:
Virtual Subnet inherits the security properties of BGP/MPLS IP VPN from RFC 4364. VPN instances provide traffic isolation between tenants, and Neighbor Discovery Proxy security considerations from RFC 6583 apply.

Inter-data-center traffic often carries sensitive information: VM migration includes private keys and configuration data. The RFC strongly recommends protecting this traffic with IPsec (RFC 4301) for confidentiality and integrity. Security mechanisms can be deployed on the PE routers or within the data centers themselves, but leaving inter-data-center traffic unprotected creates a substantial risk of exposure to pervasive monitoring.

Virtual Subnet can be deployed within a single data center as well as between locations. Service providers can adopt it incrementally by enabling it for customers or tenants that require subnet extension across facilities.
sections.eli5: Each tenant's traffic stays separate. The tunnel should be locked up so no one spies on the sensitive stuff moving between buildings. Encryption is really important here.
